title: This need comes from the will's punishment, not its nature
source_text: LXVII. Caeterum hanc delectationis coelestis necessitatem ad volendum atque operandum, & voluntatis nostrae infirmitatem, qua fit, ut nec moveri ad bonum possit, nisi quid delectaverit, nec inter duo quae delectant aliud eligere, quam quod delectando superaverit, sedulo monet author ille, non ex essentia & natura voluntatis, sed ex ejus poena proficisci. Nec enim putat hanc esse naturam humanae voluntatis absolute consideratae, ut non possit libere bonum objectum prosequi, nisi prius delectaverit: ac multo minus existimat necessarium esse, ut viso objecto bono, voluntas tangatur aliqua delectatione.
pass_a_gloss: LXVII. However this necessity of heavenly delight for willing and working, and the infirmity of our will, by which it comes about, that neither can it be moved to good, unless something has delighted, nor choose between two things which delight another than that which has prevailed by delighting, that author carefully warns proceeds not from the essence and nature of the will, but from its punishment. For he does not think this to be the nature of the human will considered absolutely, that it cannot freely pursue a good object, unless it has first delighted: and much less does he judge it necessary, that when a good object is seen, the will be touched with some delight.
pass_b_english: Thesis LXVII. That author is careful to point out that this need of heavenly delight for willing and acting, and the weakness of our will that makes it unable to be moved to the good unless something has delighted it, or to choose between two delightful things anything other than the one that has prevailed by delighting, comes not from the essence and nature of the will but from its punishment.

He does not think that the nature of the human will, considered in itself, is such that it cannot freely pursue a good object unless that object has first delighted it. Still less does he think it necessary that, when a good object is seen, the will be touched with some delight.

lemmas.latin: non ex essentia & natura voluntatis, sed ex ejus poena proficisci
lemmas.gloss: proceeds not from the essence and nature of the will, but from its punishment
the will be touched with some delight

choices.why: Jansenius ascribes the will's need of delight to the penalty of sin, not to its nature.

bible_refs: Cornelius Jansenius, Augustinus (Louvain, 1640), tome 3, De gratia Christi Salvatoris, book 4, chapters 6-9.
